text: Do you know the Statue of Liberty's skin is only about as thick as two coins?
From the ground to the tip of the torch, she stands ninety-three metres over New York Harbor.
But her copper skin is just two point four millimetres thick. The thickness of two pennies, pressed together.
So how does something that thin stand up to Atlantic storms? Look inside.
She's hollow. Holding her up is an iron skeleton, designed by Gustave Eiffel, the engineer of the Eiffel Tower.
A tall iron tower runs up the middle. From it, a web of flexible iron bars reaches out to the skin.
Eiffel made it flexible on purpose. A rigid frame would pile up stress in the copper, until it cracked.
So in strong wind, she sways. Up to three inches. And the torch up to six.
Each copper sheet was heated, then hammered into shape by hand, over wooden moulds. It's called repoussé.
When she was unveiled in eighteen eighty-six, she was shiny copper brown.
But copper reacts with the air and the sea. After nineteen hundred, a green patina spread over her.
People thought it was damage. Engineers studied it, and found the opposite. The green layer protects the copper beneath.
Thin, but protected. That's how Orbi Transfer treats your files.
Every file is locked on your own device, with AES two fifty-six, before it ever leaves.
The server only ever sees scrambled bytes. No account, no app.
